content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are dried beans to which a small amount of vegetable fat has been added to improve flavor and texture. They are rich in protein, fiber, complex carbohydrates, and provide iron, folate, and magnesium. Kidney beans are commonly used in soups, stews, salads, and vegetarian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "kidney" comes from the bean’s characteristic red‑brown spot that resembles a kidney.
Dried beans should be soaked for 6–12 hours before cooking.
Adding fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and gives the beans a richer taste.
Kidney beans are a staple in South American and Caribbean cuisines.
One serving (about 100 g dry beans) provides more than 20 g of protein.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: Kidney beans contain roughly 20 g of protein per 100 g of dry product, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, blood‑sugar regulation, and weight management.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron is essential for blood formation, while folate is important for DNA synthesis and anemia prevention.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals help maintain heart, muscle, and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic impact after cooking
items.content: When properly prepared, kidney beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Dry beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking lower its level.

items.title: Toxic lectins
items.content: Raw beans contain lectins that can cause food poisoning; they must be fully cooked.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

items.title: Higher calorie content due to added fat
items.content: The added vegetable fat increases the energy density, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak the beans for at least 6 hours, rinse well, then boil for 60–90 minutes until tender. Add them to soups, chili, salads, vegetarian patties, or serve as a side dish. The added fat makes the beans richer, so they can also be sautéed briefly after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they keep for 1–2 years. Cooked beans should be refrigerated and used within 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months.
